clinicalPearls: Half-and-half nails, or Lindsay nails, show a proximal white or dull ground-glass half sharply demarcated from a distal reddish, pink or brown half.
The distal band typically occupies from a fifth to a half of the nail length and the transverse border between the two zones is characteristically sharp.
The strongest association is with chronic kidney disease and uraemia, and the sign may be found in a substantial proportion of patients on dialysis.
The distal darker band does not fade with nail bed pressure, which helps separate it from Muehrcke lines.
It is a nail bed change (apparent leukonychia proximally with distal pigmentation) rather than a nail plate abnormality, so it does not migrate distally.
The proximal whitening is thought to relate to nail bed oedema while the distal band reflects increased melanin and capillary changes.
The sign is asymptomatic and its value is as a marker prompting assessment of renal function.
It should be distinguished from Terry nails, where the white zone is more extensive and the distal normal band much narrower.
reference.pathophysiology: Half-and-half nails are an apparent leukonychia in which the proximal portion of the nail bed becomes pale and oedematous, obscuring its normal vascular pink, while the distal portion develops a persistent darker band. The proximal whitening is attributed to oedema of the nail bed, whereas the distal brown-red band is thought to result from a combination of increased melanin deposition, thickening of the capillary walls and the concentration of the vascular bed towards the free edge. These changes are strongly linked to the metabolic and microvascular disturbances of chronic renal failure and uraemia, though the exact trigger for the melanin increase is uncertain. Because the process resides in the bed and its melanin is fixed, the distal band neither blanches with pressure nor migrates as the nail grows, distinguishing it from Muehrcke lines.
additionalInvestigations: Assessment for chronic kidney disease and dialysis status
Digital pressure (blanch) test to distinguish from Muehrcke lines
Examination of all nails for symmetry of the change
Full blood count and electrolytes as part of renal workup
redFlags: New half-and-half nails in a patient with declining renal function
Associated signs of uraemia such as pruritus, nausea or fluid overload
Rapid appearance suggesting acute deterioration of kidney function
Features overlapping with hepatic disease that might indicate Terry nails instead
reference.prognosis: The nail change is benign and needs no direct treatment, but it commonly signals chronic kidney disease and therefore follows the prognosis of the underlying renal condition. It may persist or fluctuate with the course of the renal impairment.
pitfalls: Confusing half-and-half nails with Terry nails and misdirecting investigation towards liver rather than kidney
Mistaking the distal band for Muehrcke lines by not testing whether it blanches
Overlooking the sign as a prompt to check renal function
Attributing the pigment to trauma or fungal disease
references: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology, current edition
Baran and Dawber's Diseases of the Nails and their Management, current edition
management: Reassure that the nail change itself is benign and requires no specific nail treatment
Investigate and manage the underlying chronic kidney disease and uraemia that the sign reflects
Optimise chronic kidney disease care including control of hypertension, renal anaemia and mineral bone disease
Institute renal replacement therapy with dialysis or transplantation for advanced disease, after which the nail change may improve
Distinguish the fixed distal band from Muehrcke lines using the digital blanch test
Refer to nephrology for assessment and ongoing management of the renal impairment
